headline: Tech Valuation Plunge Brings Some Opportunities
author: Michael Msika

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The sharp drop in the valuations of technology stocks, especially those linked to the artificial intelligence trade, is fueling debate over whether too much negativity has already been priced in.

The Nasdaq 100, S&P InfoTech and Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index are all trading at multiyear lows relative to expected earnings. While AI enablers such as semiconductors have taken the biggest hit, companies spending heavily on data centers did also suffer. Some more signs of capitulation this week are making the timing difficult. Yet, after strong results from Nvidia Corp., a blockbuster debut for Anthropic PBC, and an overall washed-out positioning on tech, some investors see an opportunity.
"I think we're going to have a nice AI rebound," said Louis Navellier, founder of Navellier & Associates Inc. "Earnings remain strong, but it's shocking how the valuations are so cheap right now."
Stocks including Micron Technology Inc. and Super Micro Computer Inc. are trading less than four times forecast earnings, making them "an incredible buying opportunity," he said.

The divergence between share prices and earnings expectations has been striking. Analysts are still upgrading estimates after the latest reporting season. While firms still need to deliver on those expectations, it remains to be seen how long investors can stay on the sidelines if downgrades fail to materialize.

A capex cut from hyperscalers could be a trigger for further downside, but for now their spending commitments remain firm. While the Democratic sweep in the US midterms has revived debate over the AI buildout, the shift in political control seems unlikely to halt it, even if it could slow the pace. Since the start of the year, earnings estimates for tech stocks have sharply outpaced those for the broader market, especially so for semiconductors and hardware.

"Despite these uncertainties, recent results show continued strength in cloud services and AI computing demand," said Johan Van der Biest, co-global head of equity management at Candriam, who sees potential for tech to outperform the broader market.

"Investment is translating into revenue growth, while semiconductor and equipment suppliers have issued encouraging outlooks for 2027," he said. "The current earnings picture therefore remains supportive, even as investors question the longer-term returns."

It's not just valuations that look tempting. All profits generated through leveraged exchange-traded funds this year, which have been a popular way to bet big on AI, have now nearly been erased, according to calculations by Societe Generale SA.

Derivatives strategist Jitesh Kumar looked at SOXL and TQQQ, which offer three-times leveraged exposure to chipmakers and the Nasdaq-100, respectively. A situation at the end of July when the aggregate capital invested in South Korean leveraged single-stock ETFs began losing money, "subsequently proved to be a local bottom for the underlying stocks," he said.

Both ETFs have pretty much erased all their gains for the year, even though their unleveraged underlying instruments remain up. Looking at the SOXL in particular, the 84% drawdown it has just suffered is comparable to the biggest plunges seen over the past 10 years, which were followed by sharp rebounds.

Risks to tech stocks have not disappeared. A jumbo Federal Reserve interest-rate hike in December will likely derail any rally, while three hikes are expected over the next seven months. Yet, US crude is down more than 20% in November alone, and even signs of renewed escalation have failed to push prices up meaningfully.

With valuations this low, fundamentals still strong, a global economy set to accelerate in 2027 and a full rate hike already priced in for December, investors may experience some fear of missing out. That's not even accounting for a seasonality, which is typically on equities' side in November and December.

"We think positioning is cleaner and thus entry points are more attractive," said JPMorgan Chase & Co.'s market intelligence desk led by Andrew Tyler, who sees a Fed rate hike of 50 basis points in December as highly unlikely. "While the AI trade has given the market more to think about, demand is insatiable but the pace of the build out may be slower, which is not necessarily a bad thing as the commercial adoption rate and productivity gains increase."
